blocks.title: Key vocabulary
items: g(n) — Cost so far from start.

blocks.title: Observe
blocks.text: A* orders candidate states using f(n)=g(n)+h(n), where g is known cost from the start and h estimates remaining cost to the goal.

blocks.title: Apply
blocks.text: A heuristic that never overestimates remaining true cost is admissible; with suitable search implementation/assumptions this supports optimality.

blocks.title: Evaluate
blocks.text: Track open candidates, their g/h/f and predecessors. An overestimating heuristic or incorrect update can make search miss the shortest path.

blocks.title: Worked example · Calculate all frontier f-scores
blocks.text: From P: Q has g=3,h=2,f=5 ; R has g=8,h=0,f=8 . Put both in OPEN. Choose Q next (smallest f), not simply the nearest-looking node.

blocks.title: Worked example · Improve the path to R
blocks.text: Via Q→R, new g(R)=3+2=5 , which improves the existing 8. Thus f(R)=5+0=5 , and predecessor R becomes Q. OPEN now contains R with the improved values.

questions.feedback: g(n) — Cost so far from start.

blocks.title: Compute priorities and choose
blocks.text: Calculate the two g/f pairs from the edges leaving X. State which candidate A* should expand next and why.

blocks.title: Expand Y
blocks.text: Y has g=4,h=3,f=7 , Z has g=10,h=0,f=10 , so expand Y. Via Y→Z, candidate g is 4+3=7: improve Z from 10 to 7, with predecessor Z←Y.

blocks.title: Finish the trace
blocks.text: Now Z has g=7,h=0,f=7 . Select it as the goal; predecessor chain Z←Y←X gives X→Y→Z , cost 7 . Distinguish the actual path cost g from estimated priority f.
